case_question: Two things in these libraries describe the same collection at the same time: the main surface, which draws only the members that currently qualify to be drawn, and a small secondary representation of the whole - an overview, a summary extent, a set of derived bounds - which is supposed to describe exactly what the main surface is showing. The secondary one is computed from the raw collection instead of from the qualifying subset, so the moment a member stops qualifying the two disagree: the overview is sized and positioned around members that are not being shown, and in the degenerate case where nothing qualifies it collapses onto whatever the raw collection happens to contain rather than falling back to the region the user is actually looking at. Every consumer that reads the overview to decide where the user is - a drag handle, a jump-to-fit, a scroll ratio - inherits the disagreement. The contract is that a derived summary must be computed over the same filtered set as the thing it summarises, and must have a defined answer when that set is empty. Elsewhere in the folder the same distinction is drawn on purpose: one library keeps an explicit qualifying-subset pass and hands the survivors to everything downstream, and another exposes the filtered projection of its columns as first-class accessors so that no consumer can accidentally read the unfiltered list. Which files compute a summary over the unfiltered collection, and which own the filtered-projection contract they have to be brought in line with?
